The brown notebook
It's April 2035. A small Berlin publisher has read the stories in Andrei's brown notebook — “The Stories of Kastanienallee” — and wants to publish them. Andrei and Ludwig talk about it at the café.
Ludwig, the publisher has replied. They want to do the book. In the autumn. I'm so glad I wrote the stories down back then.
Our stories. Don't forget who told them to you. I remember giving you the first notebook in October 2028.
Of course. On the cover it says: Told by Ludwig Brandt, written down by Andrei Ionescu. The editor wants to know whether it's all true.
Tell her I claim to have made up half at most. The only question is which half.
The story of the cow in Weißensee? That's from Hotte. He claims to have experienced it himself.
That one's true. Unfortunately. I wasn't there, but the whole depot laughed about it for three weeks.
The editor also wants a foreword. From you. She hopes to get a text from you. One page.
A foreword? Me? I'm a tram driver, not a writer.
You're the best storyteller I know. And it's your book. I'm just proud to have been chosen to write it down.
All right. One page. But I'll write it by hand. With Ingrid's fountain pen. And we'll dedicate the book to her.
I already have. On the first page it says: “For Ingrid, who never stopped reading.” I hope I haven't promised too much.
No, son. It's exactly right.

1. The past infinitive (Infinitiv Perfekt)
When the action in the infinitive happened BEFORE the main verb, you use the past infinitive: participle + zu + haben / sein.
Present infinitive (simultaneous)
Past infinitive (earlier)
Ich bin froh, hier zu sein.
Ich bin froh, hierher gekommen zu sein.
Er behauptet, alles zu wissen.
Er behauptet, alles gewusst zu haben.
Sie hofft, ihn zu sehen.
Sie erinnert sich, ihn gesehen zu haben.
The auxiliary (haben / sein) is the same as in the Perfekt: “Ich bin gekommen” → “gekommen zu sein”; “Ich habe gesehen” → “gesehen zu haben”.
2. dass → infinitive
When the subject is the same, the infinitive construction is more elegant than “dass”:
With dass
With an infinitive
Andrei ist froh, dass er die Geschichten aufgeschrieben hat.
Andrei ist froh, die Geschichten aufgeschrieben zu haben.
Sie bereut nicht, dass sie nach Berlin gekommen ist.
Sie bereut nicht, nach Berlin gekommen zu sein.
It doesn't work with different subjects: “Ich bin froh, dass DU gekommen bist” (not “…, gekommen zu sein”).

Das Vorwort

The brown notebook had been lying in the drawer of Andrei's desk for six and a half years, together with three others he had bought when the first one filled up. Four notebooks, more than six hundred pages, in Andrei's small, neat handwriting, in German, with a few Romanian words in the margin when the German one wouldn't come to mind. Ludwig's stories. The story of line 46 and the bell. The story of Ingrid, who had waited three days at the stop. Of Hotte and the cow. Of Friedrich and Grete and the sixty-nine years. Of Susanne and the tin box. Of Michael, of Emil and the detectives. And a hundred more.

Andrei had never thought of publishing them. He had written them down because Ludwig had told them and because he had been afraid of forgetting them. It was Lena who had come up with the idea in February, on the first night after Ingrid Hilde was born. She couldn't sleep and had read the notebooks until three in the morning, then woken Andrei and said: “These stories don't belong in a drawer. They belong to Ingrid Hilde. And to Leo. And to Elif. And to everyone who comes after us.” Andrei had said he wasn't a writer. Lena had said Ludwig wasn't either, and yet he was the best storyteller in all of Berlin.

Katrin Krüger knew a small publisher in Kreuzberg, Mrs Winter, who for thirty years had run a publishing house with three employees and made only books “that nobody else would make”. Andrei sent her fifty pages, typed up on the computer, with a letter he had rewritten seven times. For three weeks he heard nothing. Then, one Tuesday evening in April, an email came that was only three lines long: “Dear Mr Ionescu, I've read the fifty pages. Then I read them again. Please send me everything. We're doing the book.”

Andrei read the email in the bakery at five in the morning, with flour on his hands, and had to sit down on a sack of sugar, just like three years earlier when the BVG had invited him to an interview. Then he ran up to the first floor and woke Lena, and Lena read the email twice and screamed, and then they both ran back down and knocked on Ludwig's door at half past five, in their pyjamas. Ludwig opened it, his hair sticking up and Fritz beside him, and looked at them as if they had gone mad. When Andrei read him the email, he said nothing for a long time. Then he just said: “Well. Then I'll have to stop exaggerating so much. Now it's down in black and white.”

Mrs Winter came to the café a week later to meet Ludwig. She was a small, energetic woman of seventy, with short grey hair and reading glasses on a little chain round her neck, and she had a habit of jotting things down on napkins in the middle of a sentence. She drank three cups of coffee, ate two slices of apple cake and listened to Ludwig for two hours without interrupting him once. At the end she said: “Mr Brandt, I'm glad I came. I was afraid the book would be better than the storyteller. It's the other way round.” Ludwig laughed so loudly that Fritz woke up under the table.

Then they talked about the cover. Mrs Winter had brought three proposals: a photo of Kastanienallee from the eighties, a photo of the house at number thirty-one in the snow, and a photo Andrei had sent her without asking Ludwig. It was the photo from the BVG hall, taken by Kurt Wolff: Ludwig in October 2027 in the cab of the old Tatra 5218, in his BVB cap, with a grin from ear to ear. Ludwig looked at the three photos for a long time. Then he shook his head. “Definitely not that one,” he said, pointing at his own photo. “It isn't my book. It's the street's book.” Mrs Winter nodded slowly and noted something on her napkin. In the end she chose a fourth photo that nobody had suggested: the brass bell by the till in the café, with Elif's little sign underneath. “Klingeln erlaubt” (ringing allowed).

Then came the question of the foreword. Mrs Winter wanted one page, no more, from Ludwig himself, handwritten, so that she could print it in the book just as it was, with all the crossings-out. At first Ludwig said no. He said that in his whole life he had never written a text longer than a postcard, apart from two letters to a construction company and one to Susanne. Mrs Winter looked at him over her glasses. “Mr Brandt,” she said, “you claim never to have written anything. But you've told six hundred pages. Writing is just the tidying up afterwards.”

It took Ludwig three weeks to write one page. He wrote every evening, in Ingrid's armchair, with Ingrid's fountain pen, on white paper Andrei had bought. He tore up eleven drafts. Fritz lay at his feet and watched him, with the patient look of an old dog who had already seen a lot of drafts. Once Elif came by to bring him a cocoa and found him with the pen in his hand, staring at the blank sheet. “What's so hard?” she asked. Ludwig thought for a long time. “The hard part,” he said at last, “is that you can't say everything on one page. You have to decide what to leave out. And everything I leave out is a person.”

He didn't write during the day. During the day he sat in the café and told stories, as always. He wrote only in the evenings, when the house went quiet and he could hear Lena's and Andrei's footsteps above him, the music from Mara's flat on the fourth floor and sometimes, very softly, the crying of little Ingrid Hilde, which came down to him through the old walls. Those sounds, he said later, helped him write. They reminded him who he was writing for.

Grete read the manuscript too, in the weeks before the foreword, chapter by chapter; Andrei brought them to her at the care home every Wednesday after Elif's piano lesson. She read with a magnifying glass, slowly, and made little pencil marks in the margin wherever she didn't like something. At the story about herself, about the cellar in the war, the Konzerthaus and Friedrich, she made no marks at all. She handed the chapter back to Andrei and just said: “You forgot to write that I was very pretty back then. But otherwise it's all correct.” And then, more quietly: “Thank you for not forgetting him.”

Elif sat down next to him with her cocoa and thought about it, with the serious face she had learned from Grete. “Mrs Hoffmann says,” she said at last, “that a good piece doesn't have many notes. It has the right notes. And there has to be space between the notes, so the music can breathe.” Ludwig looked at her, at this ten-year-old girl who three years earlier had climbed onto a chair with a chestnut in her hand, and said: “When did you actually get so clever?” Elif shrugged. “I listened,” she said. “You taught me.”

In the end there was one page with fourteen sentences and three crossed-out words. Ludwig gave it to Andrei in an envelope, one Sunday morning, without a word, and then went out into the courtyard so as not to be there when Andrei read it. Andrei read it in the café, at Ludwig's window table, while Lena made coffee behind the counter. When he had finished, he put the sheet down on the table, took off his glasses and wiped his eyes. Lena came over and read it over his shoulder. Then she sat down beside him and neither of them said anything, and through the window you could see Ludwig in the courtyard, under the old chestnut tree that was just putting out its first leaves, pretending to watch Fritz sniffing around.

Foreword. I drove trams for forty-one years. I took millions of people from one place to another and almost never knew who they were. Only in my old age did I learn that every passenger has a story. The stories in this book aren't mine. They belong to the people of a house on Kastanienallee and of the houses next door. I only passed them on, the way you pass on a ticket when you get off. A young man from Sibiu wrote them down because he was afraid of forgetting them. I'm glad to have told him every one of them. My wife, Ingrid, taught children to read for forty years. She always said: whoever reads is never completely alone. I'm glad to have lived to see this: that our stories will now be read. Then none of us is alone. Ludwig Brandt, Kastanienallee 31, May 2035.

Mrs Winter printed the foreword exactly as it was, in Ludwig's big, crooked handwriting and with the three crossed-out words. Later Elif asked what the words had been. Ludwig smiled and said that would remain his secret. But Andrei, who kept the original in a folder, once held it up to the light and was able to read them. The first was “I”, which Ludwig had replaced with “we”. The second was “sad”, which he had replaced with “glad”. And the third, right at the end, before the signature, was a name. Ingrid. He had written it and then crossed it out, as if for a moment he had forgotten that he was the one who had to sign, not her.
